elements.text: BluTrain reward verifiers — the complete picture
Every verifier in BluTrain/RL, the async loop that runs them, the scaffolding around them, and what each one depends on
Read from RL/src/reward and RL/include/reward (working tree, 2026-11-05 23:15). Every box with a page number jumps there; the math box jumps into the separate "Math verifier, explained" drawing.

In plain words
After the model answers a prompt, a verifier compares the answer with the dataset's answer key and returns a score (usually 0 or 1). BluTrain has 7 verifier types behind one interface; a pool of reward threads runs them while generation continues, and the score lands on the last token of the trajectory for GRPO.

num_workers · timeout_s

Think of it as a factory line: the rollout worker packs each answer into a TrajectoryData, the reward loop picks the right checker for its dataset, the checker returns a ScoreResult, and the result is written where the trainer can find it.

From generated tokens to the score the trainer reads — with the exact functions and fields

In plain words
The session thread never waits for the grade: it hands the answer to the reward loop and moves on. When the grade is ready, a reward thread writes it into the TransferQueue row and the log, and the prompt's group is marked done.
gsm8k.py / dolci_think_rl.py → JSONL {prompt, input_ids, answer, data_source}
PromptRow: ground_truth, data_source → generate → token_ids (EOS included)
on_done → write_trajectory: log line + TQ row → settle
The session thread returns right after compute_score_async. Later: ReplayBufferAsync DAPO filter → RLDriver sums rm_scores per row → GRPO advantage.
rm_scores [R] f32 — verl-style outcome reward on the last token

TQ row  <uid>_<session>_0  (partition "train")
  prompts [P] · responses [R] · response_mask [R] · input_ids [P+R]
  rollout_log_probs [R] · rm_scores [R]
  extra_fields = {"reward_extra_info": {acc, pred, method, …}}
    (keys sorted, doubles %.17g, non-finite → null)
  tags: status=success · prompt_len · response_len · seq_len
        global_steps · reward_wait_ms · reward_compute_ms

rollouts_<pid>.jsonl, one line per trajectory
  time · uid · session · birth_step
  reward · gt · pred · method          (pred/method from extra_info)
  stop · response_len · undecodable_ids · mean_logprob
  reward_wait_ms · reward_compute_ms
  [reward_error] · [reward_timeout]
  prompt (session 0 only) · response

The decoded response keeps its end-of-text token. Id 50256 is inside the 50,257-entry GPT-2 vocab (its last entry decodes to <|endoftext|>) and the engines append the EOS token before stopping — so every eos-terminated response_text ends with the literal text "<|endoftext|>". gsm8k and math don't mind; exact_match and several IFEval rules do (page 13, B2).
RewardLoopWorker runs verifiers asynchronously; VerifierRegistry turns type names into verifier instances

In plain words
A small pool of reward threads grades answers in the background. If a checker crashes or takes too long, the answer simply scores 0 and training goes on. The registry is a phone book: "gsm8k" → the gsm8k checker.

constructor — optional register_extra(registry) hook (tests; verl's custom reward function), then registry.get(type) for every reward.verifiers entry → by_dataset_[dataset]. Unknown type → invalid_argument listing the known types. Duplicate dataset: last one wins silently.
num_workers > 0 → ThreadPool(num_workers) (+ Watchdog thread if timeout_s > 0). num_workers = 0 → score inline on the caller (timeout_s ignored, with a warning).
compute_score_async(traj, on_done) — verifier_for(data_source) throws before queuing if there's no entry; else enqueue run_job; the deadline is queued_at + timeout_s (queue wait counts).
run_job — skip if a timeout already finished it; score_trajectory(); std::exception → ScoreResult{} with error = e.what(); then try_emplace("acc", reward_score) — a verifier's own acc survives.
finish — atomic exchange: the first of {result, timeout} wins; an exception thrown by on_done is caught and logged so the pool thread survives.

One watchdog thread with a min-heap of (deadline, weak_ptr<Job>). On expiry: reward 0, extra_info {timeout: true, acc: 0.0}, a stderr line; the late real result is dropped. Timeout callbacks run one at a time on that thread. Default timeout_s = 0 → no deadline.

Destructor: pool_.reset() drains every queued job (their on_done still runs), then the watchdog joins. Blocking helpers compute_score / compute_score_batch wrap the async call with promise/future — never call them from on_done.

How it works
• Registered explicitly in the constructor — no static self-registration, because objects nothing references are dropped when linking from librl.a.
• get(type) builds lazily, caches, returns nullptr if unknown; register_verifier replaces and drops the cached instance; types() is sorted.
• Factories receive the RewardConfig, but make<V>() ignores it — no verifier reads config yet.
• Not thread-safe: everything is resolved in the constructor, before scoring starts.
• Not registered: code_exec, sandbox_fusion, math_equivalence.
200 async jobs: each callback once, off the caller thread
inline mode runs on the caller
0.05 s timeout vs a 300 ms verifier → one callback, timeout: true
stop_reason length scores 0 (score_trajectory); batch order kept
registry: 7 types, caching, unknown → nullptr, replacement
The reward: section, which run configs use which verifier, and who reads the scores afterwards

In plain words
A run's YAML lists which checker to use for each dataset name. Pick the wrong name and the rollout worker won't start; forget a dataset and its prompts silently fail.

reward:                                  # RLConfig.h 263-291, parser 372-401
  mode: rule_based            # rule_based | model — "model" only triggers validation
  num_workers: 8              # reward threads per RolloutWorker; 0 = inline
  timeout_s: 0.0              # 0 = no deadline
  verifiers:                  # replaces the default list entirely
    - {dataset: gsm8k, type: gsm8k}   # dataset = the row's data_source value
  detokenizer_vocab: lib/gpt2_vocab.b64   # required to decode responses
  sandbox_fusion: {url, max_concurrent: 64, memory_limit_mb: 1024}   # parsed, unused
  model: {path, enable_resource_pool: true}                          # parsed, unused
filter_groups: {enable: false, metric: reward}   # DAPO filter (replay buffer)
data: {reward_fn_key: data_source}              # JSONL column → PromptRow.data_source

Plumbing
RLDriver.cpp:168-175 creates each RolloutWorkerActor with reward.verifiers, detokenizer_vocab, rollout_data_dir, num_workers, timeout_s. RolloutWorkerActor.cpp:49-54 rebuilds RewardConfig from flat vectors — so mode, sandbox_fusion and model are not forwarded. RewardLoopManager is passed as an invalid handle (id 0).
no YAML uses the math type yet

ReplayBufferAsync::dapo_filtered
With filter_groups.enable (not on val): metric "reward" = sum of rm_scores; any other metric = extra_fields.reward_extra_info[metric] (number or bool). Groups with >1 row and all-identical values are evicted. With IFEval, acc and n_passed work as metrics.

RLDriver::compute_advantage
Sums rm_scores per row → GRPO outcome score, groups by uid prefix, logs reward/mean and reward/groups. Timing: timing/reward_wait_ms and reward_compute_ms (mean, max).

Gsm8kVerifier(bool flexible) — a port of verl's gsm8k.py with one BluTrain addition

In plain words
Finds the model's final number and compares it with the answer key as text. Strict mode wants "#### 72" or \boxed{72}; flexible mode takes the last number anywhere. "72" and "72.0" are different strings, so the second fails.
tail = last 300 BYTES of the response

strict: last match
flexible: last that isn't "" or "."
clean_number on pred AND gt: drop , $ space tab

equal strings → 1.0
else 0.0
extra_info: acc, pred

Ground truth: data_preprocess/gsm8k.py::extract_final_answer splits the reference on "####\s*", keeps the last part, strips it and removes commas → "72". gsm8k_chat.py re-templates the prompt (chat template + \boxed{} instruction) and keeps the answer.

Differences from verl's gsm8k.py
• strict also accepts \boxed{N} — added when the 1.5B model ignored "####" (GRPO_1P5B_REPORT.md bug 4)
• flexible also drops , and $; the ground truth is cleaned too (verl compares it raw)
• no format_score — always 0 when wrong · the window is bytes, not characters
The answer is 72 apples, I think
The two simplest verifiers: a whole-string comparison, and a pipeline sanity test

In plain words
exact_match says yes only if the entire response, ignoring case and extra spaces, equals the answer. short_response ignores the answer and rewards replies under 800 bytes — useful to prove the training loop works, not to teach anything.

equal → 1.0, else 0.0
no extra_info at all

Notes
• No pred, so the rollout log's pred column is empty (B7); acc is added by the loop.
• Used as the stand-in reward in test_rl_tq_end_to_end.cpp and by gpt2_single_validate.yaml on GSM8K — where whole-completion exact match is almost always 0.
• Every eos-terminated completion fails it until <|endoftext|> is stripped.

Why it exists: a trivially learnable reward independent of math ability. Per GRPO_1P5B_REPORT.md, with grpo_1p5b_sanity_short.yaml reward rose 0.35 → 0.63 and mean length fell 300 → 230 tokens over 40 steps, repeated 4 times — proof that the RL loop updates the policy. Counts bytes, including the 13-byte <|endoftext|>.
MathEquivalenceVerifier — summarized here; the full explanation is its own drawing

In plain words
The math checker reads LaTeX answers like a careful teacher: it knows \frac{1}{2} = 0.5, that sets don't care about order, and that x+1 = (x²−1)/(x−1). It is big enough to have its own 10-page drawing — the button below opens it.
Click in view mode (Ctrl+click while editing). Alt+← comes back here.
Jump straight to a page of the math drawing

Registered as type "math" (VerifierRegistry). Runs on the reward threads like every verifier; its own try/catch maps any exception to method "error", score 0. Writes extra_info acc, pred and method — the method column of rollouts_<pid>.jsonl is filled only by this verifier. Not affected by the decoded <|endoftext|> (verified). No run config uses it yet; grpo_rlvr.yaml asks for math_equivalence, which isn't registered.

Dependencies
• SymEngine (static, -fPIC, WITH_SYMENGINE_THREAD_SAFE=ON, default ~/.local/symengine) + GMP — Makefile 75-85 (SYMENGINE_LIBS appended to LDLIBS and the worker .so link)
• <regex> · MiniJson only for the CLI
• make math_verifier_cli: verifier + MiniJson + SymEngine, no CUDA/Ray — used by scripts/math_verifier_parity.py and math_verifier_metamorphic.py

As of the 16:57 source (1671 lines, 147 score assertions): exact decimals must be identical unless one has more than 6 places and they agree to ~1e-6; probing uses 7 fixed points with rtol 1e-9 (1e-4 when a side contains a written decimal); answers up to 1024 characters are parsed (kMaxAnswerLen). Still open: "dog" = "god", the % retry, same-letter choice with an unparsable value — all detailed in the math drawing.
IfEvalVerifier(bool all_or_nothing) — a C++ port of open-instruct's IFEvalVerifier over the IFEvalG constraint set

In plain words
Instruction-following prompts come with rules like "no commas", "mention 'ocean'", "under 100 words". The verifier checks each rule on the final answer and returns the fraction followed (ifeval) or 1 only if all are followed (ifeval_all).
Ground truth: Python literal → JSON, offline

Dolci row:  "[{'instruction_id': ['keywords:existence'],
              'kwargs': [{'keywords': ['ocean']}]}]"     # a Python literal

dolci_think_rl.py::ifeval_ground_truth_to_json
  ast.literal_eval → unwrap a 1-element list → json.loads if it's a string
  → require equal-length non-empty instruction_id / kwargs → json.dumps

stored:     {"instruction_id": ["keywords:existence"],
             "kwargs": [{"keywords": ["ocean"]}]}

Why offline: the C++ side reads JSON with MiniJson only. Unparseable rows are skipped and counted; --data_sources ifeval keeps only IF rows (every data_source in the file needs a reward.verifiers entry). Without the conversion every row scores 0 with error "ground_truth is not JSON".
parse ground truth (object or 1-element list) — not JSON / empty / missing lists → 0 with an error message
clean_answer: drop <|assistant|>, strip, keep text after the LAST </think>, drop <answer> / </answer>, strip  (<|endoftext|> is NOT removed)
n = min(len(ids), len(kwargs))  (Python zip) — empty answer or n = 0 → 0
each constraint → Pass / Fail / BadArgs / Unknown; only Pass counts — a broken rule never earns free reward
ifeval = passed / n   ·   ifeval_all = 1 if passed == n else 0

extra_info
  n_constraints, n_passed        int64
  pred           "2/3 failed: punctuation:no_comma"
  failed_ids · unknown_ids · bad_args_ids   (only if non-empty)
  error          (bad ground truth)
  acc            added by the loop (= the fraction)

Strict only: Google IFEval's "loose" variants (drop first/last line, remove *) are not implemented. kwargs: missing and null are the same; numbers are doubles; "less than" → <, "at least" → >=; counts that Python reads with "if not x" are BadArgs at 0.
<think>a, b, c, no ocean</think> The ocean is calm.
Code: src/reward/verifiers/IfEvalVerifier.cpp (1266 lines) · include/reward/verifiers/IfEvalVerifier.h · data_preprocess/dolci_think_rl.py · tests/unit/test_if_verifier.cpp
Every instruction id the verifier knows, grouped by family — 25 from Google IFEval, 29 from IFEvalG (Tulu / OLMo training constraints)

In plain words
Each rule is a small check on the answer text. Some just look for a character, some count words or sentences (using a port of NLTK), a few detect the language (a port of langdetect). Matching is case-sensitive unless marked ci.

keywords (10)
• existence {keywords} — each appears, ci substring
• frequency {keyword, frequency, relation} — ci count < / ≥ (also word_count_different_numbers)
• forbidden_words — none as a whole word, ci
• letter_frequency {letter, let_frequency, let_relation}
• word_once {keyword} — ci count == 1
• exclude_word_harder — " kw " never appears
• no_adjacent_consecutive — no two adjacent words start with consecutive letters
• palindrome — some word reads the same reversed
• keyword_specific_position {keyword, n, m} — token m of sentence n
• start_end — first and last word tokens equal (ci), ≥ 2 tokens

length_constraints (4)
• number_sentences {num_sentences, relation} — punkt sentences
• number_paragraphs {num_paragraphs} — split on ***
• number_words {num_words, relation} — \w+ runs
• nth_paragraph_first_word {num_paragraphs, nth_paragraph, first_word}

detectable_format (9)
• number_bullet_lists {num_bullets} — lines starting * or -
• constrained_response — "My answer is yes/no/maybe."
• number_highlighted_sections {num_highlights} — *x* and **x**
• multiple_sections {section_spliter, num_sections}
• json_format — strict JSON after stripping ``` fences
• title — <<a title>> on one line
• square_brackets — every word wrapped in [ ]
• bigram_wrapping — <<word word>> pairs
• sentence_hyphens — sentences joined by - with no spaces

detectable_content (2)
• number_placeholders {num_placeholders} — [...] spans
• postscript {postscript_marker} — P.S. / P.P.S

paragraphs (2)
• paragraphs — exactly 2 *** paragraphs
• paragraphs2 — exactly 2 blank-line paragraphs

combination (2)
• two_responses — two different parts split by ******
• repeat_prompt {prompt_to_repeat} — answer starts with the prompt

startend (2)
• end_checker {end_phrase} — ends with it (ci)
• quotation — wrapped in " "

punctuation (3)
• no_comma
• punctuation_dot — no .
• punctuation_exclamation — no !

copy (4) + new (1)
• copy:repeat_phrase {phrase, small_n} — n copies, one word changed each
• copy:copy · copy:copying_simple {prompt_to_repeat} — equal (ci)
• copy:copying_multiple {prompt_to_repeat, N} — N copies split by ******
• new:copy_span_idx {prompt_to_repeat, n_start, n_end} — a slice of the prompt

count (4)
• lowercase_counting {N} — no lowercase word more than N times
• count_increment_word {keyword1, keyword2} — once and twice
• counting_composition {n_sent, n_words} — 3 paragraphs × n sentences × n words
• count_unique — no repeated word

letters (2)
• letter_counting {N, relation} — letters (str.isalpha)
• letter_counting2 — alias of letter_frequency

change_case (3)
• capital_word_frequency {capital_frequency, capital_relation}
• english_capital — all caps AND langdetect = en
• english_lowercase — all lowercase AND langdetect = en

Phases (from the code comments): 42 rules need no tokenizer, 9 use punkt / the IFEvalG regex sentence splitter / word_tokenize, 3 use langdetect. test_if_verifier.cpp has 128 rule-level pass/fail checks covering all 54 ids, with expected values produced by running the Python reference (nltk 3.10, langdetect seed 0).

Rule examples [TEST]: keywords:frequency "concatenate" with cat ≥ 1 → Pass (substring) · forbidden_words "pineapples" vs apples → Pass (whole word) · json_format {"a": 01} → Fail · copy:repeat_phrase with no word changed → Fail · response_language "12345 !!!" → Fail (no features).
IFEval's Python dependencies, re-implemented in C++ so results match the reference exactly

In plain words
Python's IFEval leans on three libraries: NLTK to split sentences and words, langdetect to guess the language, and Python's own string rules. BluTrain re-wrote each in C++ with data tables dumped from Python, so the same text gets the same verdict.
PunktEnglishData.inc — 20,620 lines (239 KB): abbrev_types 155, collocations 36, sent_starters 38, ortho_context 20,365

sent_tokenize: Punkt (inference only, realign_boundaries) — period contexts, first pass (sentbreak, ellipsis, abbreviation), second pass (collocations, orthographic heuristic, sentence starters).
word_tokenize: NLTKWordTokenizer rules in order — starting quotes, punctuation, brackets, double dashes, ending quotes ('s 'll n't …), contractions (can|not, gon|na, wan|na, 't|is …). Each re.sub is a hand-written scanner: std::regex has no lookbehind or Unicode \w.
LangdetectData.inc — 184,357 lines (1.86 MB): 55 language profiles + normalization tables

langdetect 1.0.9: strip URLs/emails, normalize (Vietnamese diacritics, CJK classes), 1-3-gram extraction (skipped inside ALL-CAPS words), 7 trials with CPython's MT19937 seeded 0 + random.gauss, Neumaier-compensated normalization every 5 steps, stop at p > 0.99999 or 1000 iterations; best language above 0.1.
PyStrTables.inc — 794 lines (99 KB), dumped from Python 3.12.13 / unicodedata 15.0.0 / regex 2026.9.29

Python str semantics on UTF-8: decode (bad bytes → U+FFFD) and encode; re-module and regex-module \w \d \s; isalpha / isalnum / isupper / islower / istitle; single-code-point lower; strip, sub, replace_all, split.
I can't do it, won't you? They're gonna say 'hello' (maybe).
I ca n't do it , wo n't you ? They 're gon na say ' hello ' ( maybe ) .
Dr. Smith arrived at 3 p.m. today. He said: wow! Is it e.g. fine?
punkt: 4 sentences, splitting after "e.g." — the IFEvalG regex splitter gives 3
Bonjour, comment allez-vous aujourd'hui? · Hola, ¿cómo estás?
vi — ALL-CAPS words are skipped, so too few n-grams remain
no features → response_language fails (Python IFEval counts it as passed)
Missing from the repo: the generator scripts for all three .inc tables — only header comments describe how they were dumped (B14).
Deliberate differences from the Python reference
keywords, phrases and markers are matched literally (Python treats them as regexes: "c++" raises, "." matches anything) — postscript keeps . as a wildcard
missing / null kwargs and 0 counts are BadArgs (fail) — Python's build_description would draw random values
unknown ids and bad kwargs fail that one constraint — Python's verifier crashes
langdetect "no features" is a Fail (IFEval returns True) and is deterministic (seed 0, sorted profiles)
case folding for keyword search is ASCII-only; other comparisons use Unicode single-character lower
strict only — no loose mode · ground truth must be JSON (conversion moved offline)

In plain words
Some reward classes are placeholders for later work: they exist so the design compiles, but calling them throws "not implemented yet". This page separates them from what actually runs.

Two dispatch policies: streaming random.choice per trajectory, or colocated chunk → scatter → gather (verl reward_loop.py 342-360). Rule-based verifiers need no resource pool; a reward model must have its own (enable_resource_pool, copied from verl). Plan order: exact-match and math first, code-exec in a security-reviewed workstream, reward model optional.

Known issues found by reading and running the code, most severe first

In plain words
Two of these can silently cost reward right now: the end-of-text token glued to every answer (B2), and prompts whose dataset has no verifier failing without a log line (B3).

B1 · grpo_rlvr.yaml names unregistered types
math_equivalence and code_exec parse fine but make RolloutWorker throw at construction. The registered math type is "math"; code-exec isn't registered.

B2 · the decoded EOS reaches every verifier
"<|endoftext|>" ends every eos-terminated response. Breaks exact_match and IFEval end/case rules (quotation, end_checker, last_word, json_format, english_capital: all 1 → 0 [RAN]), adds 13 bytes to short_response. gsm8k and math unaffected. Fix: strip special tokens in agent_loop_postprocess or clean_answer.

B3 · unknown data_source fails silently
verifier_for throws inside agent_loop_postprocess; run_prompt's catch settles the session as failed with no log line → failure groups, evicted and refilled.

B4 · missing detokenizer_vocab
every session throws (gpt2_single_validate.yaml) — also silently.

B5 · gsm8k string-compare quirks
"72." captured with its period; flexible's lone "," → empty pred; \boxed{ 72 } not matched; 1.50 ≠ 1.5; window counts bytes.

B6 · misleading "verifier threw" log
run_job logs it whenever extra_info has "error" — including IFEval's normal ground-truth errors.

B7 · exact_match sets no pred
the rollout log's pred column is always empty for it.

B8 · IFEval zip truncation
mismatched instruction_id / kwargs lengths drop constraints (same as Python; dolci_think_rl.py guards it).

B9 · duplicate reward.verifiers datasets
the last entry wins without a warning.

B10 · non-numeric DAPO metric
filter_groups.metric naming pred or failed_ids makes ReplayBufferAsync throw "missing DAPO metric".

B11 · timeout semantics
the deadline includes queue wait; timeout callbacks run serially; inline mode ignores timeout_s.

B12 · settings dropped or unused
